proposals.title: Domain-Adaptive Deep Classifier to Reduce Misgraded Apple Returns on a Sorting Line
proposals.markdown:
## Domain-Adaptive Deep Classifier to Reduce Misgraded Apple Returns on a Sorting Line

**Company:** Described problem works in prerada hrane. [C999] Challenge C999-CH1.  
**Researcher:** Nikola Stojanović is an Associate Professor in the Department of Computing and Control Engineering, Faculty of Technical Sciences. [R0548]  
**Format:** joint project, one page.

### The problem
The company's sorting line uses a fixed-threshold camera system that reaches only ~88% accuracy on apple grading, causing customer returns of misclassified fruit. [C999-CH1] The two defect types driving misclassification are minor bark damage and early rot, which the current rule-based thresholds cannot reliably separate. [C999-CH1] The company holds 40,000 labeled apple images collected across three harvest seasons, but the fixed-threshold system does not exploit them. [C999-CH1]

### Prior work
- A 2022 study reports 92.42% average accuracy on apple defect classification using semantic segmentation combined with a pruned YOLO V4 detector on a conveyor system. [W4304128474]
- A 2022 study reports 94.8% accuracy in classifying apple decay and bruise under uneven illumination using texture features and an SVM model. [W4206192560]

### Research questions
1. Can a deep classifier trained with domain randomisation on the three-season image archive exceed 88% accuracy on bark-damage and early-rot cases, measured by precision, recall and F1 against the company's labelled hold-out set from the most recent season?
2. Can active learning, applied to the existing 40,000 labelled images, identify and prioritise the hardest bark-damage and early-rot cases so that a targeted re-annotation round of under 2,000 images yields a measurable accuracy gain over the baseline classifier?

### Approach
- Train a baseline deep classifier on the full 40,000-image archive, stratified by harvest season, to establish the current accuracy ceiling and identify which defect classes and seasonal splits drive the most errors.
- Apply domain randomisation techniques—colour-jitter, lighting simulation and texture augmentation—to the training data to reduce the seasonal appearance shift that causes the fixed-threshold system to fail across harvests.
- Use the active learning framework based on ensemble uncertainty and diversity sampling to score the existing labelled set, surface the hardest bark-damage and early-rot images, and run a targeted re-annotation pass of the highest-uncertainty cases.
- Evaluate the final classifier on the sorting-line camera stream, measuring accuracy, precision and recall per defect class against the labelled hold-out set, with the target of exceeding the current 88% accuracy baseline.

### Plan

| Period | Work | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Months 1–3 | A master's student from the researcher's group, supervised by Stojanović and one company engineer (20% time), audits and splits the 40,000-image archive by season and defect class, trains a baseline CNN classifier, and logs per-class error rates. | Baseline accuracy report; stratified train/validation/test splits; ranked list of failure modes by defect class and season. |
| Months 4–6 | The master's student applies domain randomisation augmentations and retrains the classifier; the active learning pipeline scores the full labelled archive and surfaces the top uncertain bark-damage and early-rot cases for a company re-annotation pass. | Improved classifier exceeding 88% accuracy on the hold-out test set; shortlist of up to 2,000 images flagged for re-annotation. |
| Months 7–9 | The retrained model (using re-annotated hard cases) is validated against the sorting-line camera stream; the company engineer integrates the model into the existing camera software; final accuracy, precision and recall are recorded per defect class. | Production-ready model deployed on the sorting line; technical report with per-class metrics; one joint conference or journal paper submitted. |

### First six months
- Week 1–2: The company transfers the 40,000 labeled images (with season and defect-class metadata) to the researcher's group under a signed data-sharing agreement; the master's student sets up the training environment.
- Month 1: The master's student audits label quality, splits the archive into season-stratified train/validation/test sets, and confirms the class distribution of bark-damage and early-rot images.
- Month 2–3: Baseline CNN classifier trained and evaluated; per-class and per-season error rates documented and shared with the company engineer for review.
- Month 4–5: Domain randomisation augmentations applied; active learning pipeline run on the full labelled archive; company engineer reviews the flagged hard cases and confirms re-annotation priority list.

### What each side brings
- **Company:** 40,000 labeled apple images from three harvest seasons, with defect-class annotations, available for model training and validation. [C999-CH1]
- **Faculty:** Stojanović co-authored domain randomisation methods for cross-domain transfer in visual defect detection across different material types and manufacturing processes. [SYN-PUB-06393] Stojanović co-authored an active learning framework using ensemble uncertainty and diversity sampling to optimise annotation effort in defect detection. [SYN-PUB-06396] Stojanović co-authored few-shot surface defect detection combining preprocessing with prototypical networks on reflective metal parts. [SYN-PUB-06388] Stojanović leads algorithm development and validation in the VISIONQC project, which develops a modular inspection platform for SMEs with minimal labeled data requirements and includes pilot deployments at regional manufacturing SMEs. [SYN-PRJ-0011]

### Why this pair
The company has a well-defined accuracy gap (88%), three seasons of labelled data, and a sorting line with a camera system—the conditions needed to train and test a classifier. Stojanović brings domain randomisation for cross-domain transfer in visual defect detection and active learning to prioritise annotation effort on the hard bark-damage and early-rot cases in the existing archive. Neither side could do it alone: the company provides the only asset that makes the result credible on a real sorting line (production images and live camera hardware), while the researcher provides the methods that turn that archive into a classifier that generalises.

- The sorting line's fixed-threshold system reaches only ~88% accuracy, and Stojanović co-authored domain randomisation for cross-domain visual transfer in defect detection. [C999-CH1, SYN-PUB-06393]
- Bark-damage and early-rot are the defect types driving misclassification on the sorting line, and Stojanović co-authored an active learning framework that prioritises uncertain cases to optimise annotation effort. [C999-CH1, SYN-PUB-06396]
- The VISIONQC project develops a modular inspection platform for SMEs with minimal labelled data requirements and includes pilot deployments at regional manufacturing SMEs. [SYN-PRJ-0011]

### Risks and constraints
- Stojanović's cited defect detection publications cover reflective metal parts, polymer assembly-line components, and manufacturing processes; none covers organic produce or food-surface texture. [SYN-PUB-06388, SYN-PUB-06391, SYN-PUB-06393]
- The active learning framework (SYN-PUB-06396) is validated with industrial partners producing metal stampings and injection-moulded plastic components; the record does not cover multi-season labeled datasets of organic produce. [SYN-PUB-06396]

### Agreed up front (proposed)
- Publication: results may be published after a 30-day review by the company; the company may request removal of commercially sensitive sorting-line parameters before submission.
- Ownership: the company owns the trained model weights and any integrated software; the researcher's group retains the domain randomisation and active learning code as general-purpose research tools.
- Data access: the company provides the 40,000-image archive to the researcher's group for the duration of the project under a data-sharing agreement; images are stored on the researcher's institutional servers and deleted or returned at project close.
- Preconditions: the data-sharing agreement is signed and the image archive is transferred before the master's student begins Month 1 work; the company names one engineer as the day-to-day contact for re-annotation and camera integration.

### Sources
- C999: Described problem
- C999-CH1: Naša linija za sortiranje voća često pogrešno razvrstava jabuke sa sitnim oštećenjima kore i početnom truleži.
- R0548: Nikola Stojanović
- SYN-PRJ-0011: VISIONQC: AI quality control for SMEs (2023)
- SYN-PUB-06388: Few-shot surface defect detection on reflective metal parts (2024)
- SYN-PUB-06391: Adaptive anomaly detection for multi-product assembly lines using one-class contrastive learning (2024)
- SYN-PUB-06393: Domain randomization strategies for cross-industry transfer in visual defect detection (2022)
- SYN-PUB-06396: Active learning with model uncertainty sampling for efficient annotation in industrial inspection pipelines (2021)
- W4206192560: Extraction and classification of apple defects under uneven illumination based on machine vision (2022) https://openalex.org/W4206192560
- W4304128474: Real-Time Grading of Defect Apples Using Semantic Segmentation Combination with a Pruned YOLO V4 Network (2022) https://openalex.org/W4304128474

claim.text: System must handle apples with minor bark damage and early rot, which are difficult to distinguish from acceptable fruit

rejected.reason: C999-CH1 states the line misclassifies apples with minor bark damage and early rot, but it does not say these are 'difficult to distinguish from acceptable fruit' — that characterisation is not in the source.

claim.text: Training data spans three harvest seasons, suggesting seasonal variation in appearance may affect model generalization

rejected.reason: C999-CH1 states only that the images come from three harvest seasons; it does not mention or imply seasonal variation in appearance or its effect on model generalization — that inference is added beyond what the text states.

claim.text: Leads the VISIONQC project, which develops modular AI-powered inspection platforms for SME manufacturers with minimal labeled data requirements.

rejected.reason: SYN-PRJ-0011 states that VISIONQC develops a modular inspection platform for SMEs with minimal labeled data, but it does not say Stojanović 'leads' the project—it says he is the academic partner who leads algorithm development and validation; the claim that he 'leads the VISIONQC project' overstates his role as described.

claim.text: Automated optical inspection system selection, integration, and benchmarking methodology for electronics manufacturing quality control

rejected.reason: SYN-PUB-05242 surveys few-shot and transfer learning for visual inspection in electronics manufacturing but does not cover AOI system selection, integration, or benchmarking methodology; SYN-PRJ-0371 covers benchmark dataset construction and evaluation protocols but not AOI system selection or integration — neither cited source supports 'system selection, integration, and benchmarking methodology' as a combined topic.

claim.text: Operates a dedicated machine-vision laboratory equipped with a programmable X-ray inspection rig, three high-resolution industrial cameras, and a GPU cluster available for access arrangements with NTP companies on a scheduled basis

rejected.reason: R0437 states the group operates a dedicated machine-vision laboratory equipped with a programmable X-ray inspection rig, three high-resolution industrial cameras, and a cluster of GPU workstations, and that the X-ray rig is available for access arrangements with NTP companies on a scheduled basis — but the record says 'GPU cluster' is for training/evaluation, not explicitly listed as available for NTP access arrangements (only the X-ray rig is mentioned for NTP access), and the claim says 'GPU cluster available for access arrangements' which adds a fact not directly in the text for the GPU cluster specifically.

claim.text: 2D code detection on curved surfaces under industrial lighting conditions using deep learning and signal processing.

rejected.reason: Neither SYN-PUB-06942 nor SYN-PUB-06938 mentions 'deep learning' or 'signal processing'; SYN-PUB-06942 reports baseline results from open-source pipelines (e.g., ZXing-C++) and SYN-PUB-06938 uses projective rectification and adaptive thresholding, so these two methods named in the claim are not in the cited texts.

claim.text: Real-time barcode localisation on cylindrical and curved packaging using projective rectification and embedded vision hardware.

rejected.reason: SYN-PAT-048 covers cylindrical containers only, and SYN-PUB-06938 covers cylindrical beverage cans only; neither cited source mentions 'curved packaging' as a distinct surface type beyond cylindrical, so the claim widens the scope beyond what the texts state.

claim.text: Multi-sensor fusion for material sorting, including combination of NIR with Raman spectroscopy and structured-light height measurement, with decision-level and signal-level fusion architectures.

rejected.reason: SYN-PUB-06123 covers NIR with Raman decision fusion; SYN-PUB-06121 covers structured-light height measurement combined with NIR; SYN-PRJ-0328 covers sensor fusion strategies including NIR, Raman, and XRF; however, the claim states both 'decision-level and signal-level fusion architectures' but SYN-PUB-06121 covers spatial/geometric calibration using structured light rather than signal-level fusion of NIR with structured light for material classification, and SYN-PRJ-0328 mentions a 'comparative evaluation report on sensor fusion architectures' without specifying decision-level vs signal-level fusion.

claim.text: Unsupervised domain adaptation and concept drift compensation using kernel mean matching and conformal prediction for maintaining classifier performance under distribution shift.

rejected.reason: SYN-PUB-06122 covers unsupervised drift compensation using kernel mean matching; SYN-PUB-06124 covers conformal prediction for recycled content estimation (regression), not classifier performance under distribution shift; SYN-PAT-032 covers kernel mean matching for spectral drift compensation; however, the claim pairs conformal prediction with 'concept drift compensation for maintaining classifier performance under distribution shift,' but SYN-PUB-06124 applies conformal prediction to regression prediction intervals for recycled content, not to domain adaptation or distribution shift compensation.

claim.text: Led the NIR sensor integration work package in the cross-border Interreg IPA CIRCPACK project coordinating with Hungarian and Serbian waste management partners on pilot sorting line deployment and spectral library harmonisation.

rejected.reason: SYN-PRJ-0328 identifies Krstić (R0521) as work package leader on NIR sensor integration in the Interreg IPA CIRCPACK project coordinating with Hungarian partners, but the project description mentions Hungarian and Serbian partners on dataset harmonisation and shared spectral libraries — it does not describe the partners as 'waste management partners' specifically for the Hungarian side (Óbuda University is a university, not a waste management company), and 'spectral library harmonisation' maps to 'shared spectral libraries' and 'dataset harmonisation,' but the claim says 'Hungarian and Serbian waste management partners' when Óbuda University is not a waste management company.

claim.text: Crack, spalling, corrosion, efflorescence, and impact damage detection and segmentation in reinforced concrete, masonry, and steel structures using ResNet, EfficientNet, DeepLabV3+, and VGG-16 backbones.

claim.text: Domain adaptation for visual inspection tasks using adversarial feature alignment for camera model shift, pseudo-label refinement for altitude-dependent resolution and collection condition shift, and contrastive pre-training on synthetic renders.
